segments: Think of who you were ten years ago.
That comes easily:
you can see the clothes,
you can still hear the song you
played until the people around you
begged you to stop,
and you can feel exactly how certain
you were about a person,
or a job, or a plan
that was going to work out.
Now turn around and face the other way.
Picture who you will be ten years from now.
Notice what happens:
the picture goes soft at the edges.
You can manage a rough sketch,
but it is mostly this person again,
in slightly better shoes,
holding slightly more money,
with all the same opinions
professionally upholstered.
Some part of you has quietly decided
that the changing is over,
and that the person who shows up in
ten years will be,
more or less, the one sitting here tonight.
That decision is wrong at every age,
and it has a name.
three researchers put the question to
more than nineteen thousand people,
aged eighteen to sixty-eight.
They asked one group how much they
had changed in the past ten years.
They asked another group how much
they expected to change in the next ten.
They asked about personality and about values,
and then they asked about plain taste:
the favourite food,
the favourite hobby, the closest friend.
Almost everyone said the same two things.
I have changed a great deal.
And I am now, at last,
finished.
The eighteen-year-olds said it,
the forty-year-olds said it,
and the sixty-eight-year-olds said it.
Every group could see the
road behind them in detail,
and every group was confident the
road ahead ran straight.
They called it the end of history illusion.
You keep deciding that history is the
thing that already happened to you.
So why would the same
mistake turn up at every age?
Because the two
questions are not the same job.
Remembering is reading,
because the past is written down
already and you only have to look it up.
Predicting is writing,
because you have to build a whole
person who does not exist yet,
and you have to do it out of nothing.
One of those is easy.
One of those is work.
And when the work is hard,
the mind does something unhelpful
with the empty space:
it treats the blank as an answer.
It does not report that
the picture is missing. It reports,
with enormous confidence,
that nothing much is coming.
You have felt this from the other side.
Think of whatever changed you most in
the last ten years,
and ask whether you saw it coming.
Almost nobody does. It arrived,
and then it was obvious,
and the obviousness arranged itself
backwards until it seemed to have
been there all along.
There is a second failure sitting
underneath the first one,
and it belongs to the same two researchers.
Suppose someone handed you the future.
You get to see the events,
all of them, in order.
The job you lose.
The person who leaves.
The thing you have been dreading,
arriving exactly as dreaded.
You would still get it wrong.
Not the events. The weather.
You would badly overestimate how long
each one was going to hurt.
Gilbert and Wilson called
this the durability bias,
and they found it everywhere they looked:
in people imagining a breakup,
a rejected job application,
an election going the wrong way,
a denial of tenure.
In every case the forecast was
roughly right about the direction and
badly wrong about the duration.
People expected to be levelled,
and they were levelled, briefly,
and then they were mostly fine.
The reason is almost embarrassing:
you have a psychological immune system,
and when something bad happens it
goes to work immediately,
without asking you first.
You find the reason it
was probably for the best,
and you notice all the ways that
person was wrong for you anyway.
You quietly rewrite the job you did
not get into a job you never wanted.
It is not lying, exactly.
It is maintenance.
And like your other immune system,
you cannot feel it running.
So when you picture next year,
you picture the wound without the healing.
You see yourself standing out in the rain,
and you forget that you own a coat,
and that you will put it on,
and that you will barely remember being wet.
Which is the first mistake again,
pointed somewhere new.
You are not only bad at
picturing who you will be.
You are bad at picturing how that
person will feel,
and you get it wrong in one direction.
You underestimate them.
The future you is tougher than you think,
and you will not give
them the credit in advance.
Now the part that most retellings leave out:
the study has problems,
and they are worth saying out loud.
It did not follow the
same people for ten years;
it asked different people of
different ages on a single afternoon
and lined the answers up.
It leaned on memory,
and memory flatters,
because you are the one grading your own past.
And there is a sharper objection.
Suppose you know that you will change,
but you have no idea which way.
What is your best guess for the
person you will be?
It is the person you are now.
Not because you lack imagination,
but because that is the smart bet.
So part of this famous effect may be
arithmetic rather than blindness.
What survives is smaller
and still worth having:
change is far easier to see behind
you than in front of you.
The researchers went further,
and put a price on that gap.
They asked people what they would pay
to see their favourite band play in ten years,
and the answer came back at a hundred
and twenty-nine dollars.
Then they asked what those same
people would pay to see the band they
loved ten years ago play tonight.
Eighty dollars.
Same money, same seat, same band.
The only thing that changed was which
way you were facing in time.
You will happily buy a ticket for a stranger,
as long as the stranger is you.
That is the quiet cost of it.
You sign the lease,
take the job and book the ten-year plan,
and you price every one of them for
the person standing here tonight.
So here is the part you can use.
You are not the final draft.
The taste you would defend tonight,
the plan you are certain of,
the person you cannot imagine living without —
some of that is scaffolding,
and scaffolding comes down.
Treat who you are now as a reasonable
working estimate rather than a verdict,
make the promises you can actually keep,
and hold the rest a little more loosely.
You are not finished.
You are the most recent version,
and the next one is already on the way.
